books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

primary_sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854)

stimulus.text: Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854): "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." Thoreau built a cabin at Walden Pond near Concord, Massachusetts, and lived there for two years, from 1845 to 1847.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim quotation from Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854). Public domain; wording checked against the published text. The cabin dates are from the book's account.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Thoreau went to the woods mainly to do which of the following?

options.text: Survey land for a new railroad
options.misconception: Thoreau lived near a growing town, so it is easy to tie him to its building projects.

options.text: Hide from the government after committing a crime
options.misconception: Thoreau later went to jail, so it is easy to move that jail stay to the start of the story.

options.text: Live simply and learn what life truly required

options.misconception: Thoreau grew beans at the pond, so it is easy to think he wrote a farming manual.

rationales.A: Thoreau built a cabin to live in, not to survey a railroad line.
rationales.B: The jail stay came later, over a tax; the woods came first, as an experiment in living.
rationales.C: 'Live deliberately' and 'the essential facts of life' say it plainly: strip life down and see what it teaches.
rationales.D: Thoreau farmed a little to feed himself, but Walden is a book about living, not a farmer's guide.
rationales.general:
1. Read the quote slowly. 'Live deliberately' and 'the essential facts of life' are the whole purpose.
2. Match the purpose to the act. A cabin, two years, few possessions — an experiment in simple living.
Background: Thoreau lived at the pond from 1845 to 1847 and wrote Walden about it.
Remember: when an author states his purpose in his own words, take him at his word.
